tips.title: Red-shift is an increase in wavelength
tips.body: Red-shift is **an observed increase in the wavelength** of light from distant galaxies. Say **increase in wavelength**, not "the light looks red" — the wavelength is the measurement, and it is what the mark scheme wants.

tips.title: Further, faster, bigger shift
tips.body: **The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.** Three things rising together — learn them as one sentence and most questions on this topic answer themselves.

tips.title: Space itself is expanding
tips.body: Red-shift is evidence that **space itself (the universe) is expanding** — not that galaxies are flying outwards through space from a point. This distinction is examined, and it also explains why the expansion looks the same from everywhere.

tips.title: The Big Bang is a model, not a bang
tips.body: **The Big Bang theory suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.** It does not describe an explosion **in** space; it describes space itself expanding **from** that state.

tips.title: Since 1998, faster still
tips.body: **Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.** That is a separate, later finding from red-shift itself, and it is why **dark energy** is discussed.

why.matters:
The light from distant galaxies arrives with its wavelengths stretched, and the further the galaxy, the more stretched it is. From that one measurement comes the largest claim in the course: that space itself is expanding, and so was once far smaller, hotter and denser than it is now.

The topic is as much about how science gets from an observation to a theory as about the theory, and about what the theory still cannot explain.

examples.title: The siren that drops as the ambulance passes
examples.body:
As an ambulance goes past, the siren's note drops. Waves from something moving away from you arrive stretched out, with a longer wavelength, and for sound a longer wavelength is a lower note.

Red-shift is the same reading taken from light. The pattern of lines in a galaxy's spectrum arrives shifted towards longer wavelengths, the red end, and the shift says the galaxy is receding. The cause is different, because for galaxies it is the space between us that is stretching rather than the galaxy driving off, but what an astronomer measures is exactly what your ear measures on the pavement: a wavelength longer than it should be.

props.title: Two versions of the same reading

visual.alt: A table comparing the drop in a passing siren's note, a longer wavelength because the source is moving away, with red-shift, the longer wavelength of light from a receding galaxy

examples.title: The raisin loaf
examples.body:
Why should the further galaxies be the faster ones? Put raisins in a loaf of dough at 1 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm from one raisin you pick as yours, and let the loaf double in size in the oven.

The raisin that was 1 cm away is now 2 cm away: it moved 1 cm. The one at 5 cm is now at 10 cm: it moved 5 cm in the same time, five times as fast. Nothing pushed them; the dough grew. That is the specification's sentence, that space itself is expanding, and why no raisin is the centre.

visual.alt: A table of three raisins at one, three and five centimetres from yours in a loaf that doubles in size, ending at two, six and ten centimetres, so the furthest moved furthest in the same time

examples.title: The Sun you see is eight minutes old
examples.body:
Light is fast but not instant. Light covers the $384$ million metres from the Moon at $3 \times 10^8$ m/s, which takes about 1.3 s. From the Sun, 150 million kilometres away, about 8 minutes. If the Sun went out you would not know for eight minutes.

The further the object, the older the light. The nearest other star's light is years old, and the light from a distant galaxy set off before there was an Earth. So the red-shifted galaxies are not only far away; they are the universe as it used to be. Looking out is looking back, and that is why old light can carry evidence about a beginning.

props.title: How old the light is when it reaches you

visual.alt: A table showing that light from the Moon takes about one point three seconds to arrive, from the Sun about eight minutes, and from the nearest other star about four years

steps.title: Red-shift
steps.body:
**There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.** This effect is called **red-shift**.

**Why "red".** Within visible light, **red** has the **longest** wavelength. So light whose wavelength has been **increased** has moved **towards the red end** of the spectrum — hence the name.

**What is actually measured.** Astronomers do not judge this by eye. Each element absorbs and emits light at very **specific wavelengths**, producing a pattern of lines in a spectrum. That pattern is known precisely from laboratory work on Earth. In light from a distant galaxy the **same pattern** appears, but every line is shifted **towards longer wavelengths**. Because the pattern is recognisable, the **size of the shift** can be measured exactly.

**The key observation**, in the specification's own words:

> **The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.**

Three things rise together — **distance**, **speed of recession**, and **size of the red-shift**. A galaxy four times as far away is moving about four times as fast and shows about four times the shift.

**Nearly all galaxies show red-shift**, meaning almost everything is moving **away** from us. The word "most" in the specification matters: a few of the very nearest galaxies are moving **towards** us, because local gravitational attraction outweighs the expansion at short range.

props.title: Four times as far means about four times as fast, and four times the shift

visuals.alt: A table of three galaxies showing that speed of recession and red-shift both rise in proportion to distance

check.prompt: Red-shift is an observed increase in which property of light?
check.solution: An observed **increase in wavelength**. Red has the longest wavelength in visible light, which is where the name comes from.

steps.title: What red-shift tells us
steps.body:
**The observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding, and supports the Big Bang theory.**

**Read that carefully: space itself.** It is tempting to picture galaxies hurtling outwards through space from some central point, like debris from an explosion. That is **not** what the evidence indicates. **Space between the galaxies is stretching**, carrying the galaxies apart with it.

**Why the distinction matters** — and it is examined. If galaxies were flying outwards from a point, we could work out where that point was, and we would appear to be near it since everything recedes from us. But **every** observer in **every** galaxy sees the same thing: everything receding, and the most distant receding fastest.

That is exactly what **expanding space** predicts. If all distances stretch by the same proportion, then from any viewpoint the furthest objects move away fastest, because there is **more space in between to stretch**. So there is **no centre** — and the fact that the universe looks the same from everywhere is a consequence, not a coincidence.

**Why greater distance means greater speed** follows directly. Twice as much space between us and a galaxy means twice as much stretching each second, so it recedes twice as fast. That is precisely the **further, faster** relationship that is observed — which is why the observation is such strong support for the model.

**Running it backwards.** If everything is spreading apart now, then in the past everything was **closer together** — and further back still, closer yet. That line of reasoning leads to the Big Bang.

steps.title: From observation to theory
steps.body: **The specification asks how scientists are able to use observations to arrive at theories such as the Big Bang theory.** Working through the chain is the best way to see it.

steps.title: Accelerating expansion, and what is unknown
steps.body:
**Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.**

**This is a separate finding from red-shift itself**, and a much more recent one. Red-shift established that the universe is **expanding**. The supernova observations suggest the expansion is **accelerating** — galaxies are not merely receding, but receding **faster over time**.

**Why supernovae were used.** A particular kind of exploding star has a known, consistent brightness, so comparing how bright it **appears** with how bright it **actually is** gives its **distance**. Combining that with its red-shift lets astronomers reconstruct how the expansion rate has changed over the history of the universe.

**Why it was surprising.** Gravity pulls all matter together, so the expansion was expected to be **slowing down**. Finding it speeding up meant something was missing from the model.

**There is still much about the universe that is not understood**, and the specification names two examples.

**Dark mass** (often called dark matter) **bends light and holds galaxies together but does not emit electromagnetic radiation** — so it cannot be seen directly. Its presence is inferred from its **gravitational effects**: galaxies rotate as though they contain far more mass than is visible.

**Dark energy** is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion to **accelerate**. Naming it is not the same as explaining it — the name records that something is happening that is not yet understood.

**That is a fair picture of science**, and the specification asks you to appreciate it. The Big Bang model is very well supported by evidence, and at the same time **large questions remain open**. Both things are true at once.

steps.body:

2. What does red-shift provide evidence for?

**Part C.**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Define red-shift as an increase in wavelength.** Not "the light turns red" and not "the light gets redder". The measurable quantity is the **wavelength**, and it **increases**.

**Give all three parts of the key observation.** **The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving, and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.** Many answers give distance and speed and drop the shift, or give the shift without the distance relationship — and it is the **relationship** that carries the argument.

**Say space itself is expanding.** Red-shift is evidence that **space itself (the universe) is expanding**, not that galaxies are flying outwards through space from a centre. This is the single most common misconception in the topic.

**Use the no-centre argument.** If galaxies were flying from a point, we would seem to be near it. But **every** observer sees everything receding, with the most distant fastest — which is exactly what **uniformly stretching space** produces. There is **no centre**, and saying why is a strong answer.

**Explain further-means-faster mechanically.** More space between two galaxies means **more space stretching** each second, so the separation grows faster. That turns an observed correlation into an explanation.

**Distinguish the two findings.** **Red-shift** shows the universe is **expanding**. **Supernova observations since 1998** suggest it is **accelerating**. Different evidence, different conclusions, different decades — and the second was a surprise, since gravity should have been slowing things down.

**Describe dark mass by what it does.** It **bends light and holds galaxies together but does not emit electromagnetic radiation**, so it is detected only through its **gravitational effects**. Note that naming **dark energy** does not explain it — the name marks the gap rather than filling it.

**Show how a theory is built.** **Observation first**, then interpretation, then a model, then extrapolation — and the model stands only while it keeps fitting. The specification asks explicitly how scientists **use observations to arrive at theories**, and it also asks you to acknowledge that **much about the universe is still not understood**. A confident answer holds both: the Big Bang model is very well supported, **and** large questions remain open.

steps.body:
- **Red-shift** is an observed **increase in the wavelength** of light from most distant galaxies.
- Red has the **longest wavelength** in visible light, hence the name.
- It is measured by comparing **spectral line patterns** with known laboratory values.
- **The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the increase in wavelength.**
- Red-shift is evidence that **space itself (the universe) is expanding**.
- Galaxies are **not** flying outwards through space from a centre.
- There is **no centre**: uniformly stretching space looks the same from **everywhere**.
- **More space between** means **more stretching**, which is why distance and speed rise together.
- Running the expansion **backwards** means everything was once much closer.
- **The Big Bang theory suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.**
- **Since 1998**, observations of **supernovae** suggest distant galaxies are **receding ever faster**.
- That **acceleration** is a separate, later finding from red-shift itself.
- **Dark mass** bends light and holds galaxies together but **emits no electromagnetic radiation**.
- **Dark energy** is the name for whatever drives the acceleration.
- **There is still much about the universe that is not understood.**

questions.prompt: Explain what red-shift is, what it shows about the universe, and how it provides evidence for the Big Bang theory.
questions.solution:
**Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.** The name comes from the fact that **red has the longest wavelength** in visible light, so light whose wavelength has increased has shifted **towards the red end** of the spectrum.

**It is a measurement, not an impression.** Each element absorbs and emits light at very specific wavelengths, giving a distinctive pattern of lines in a spectrum, and those wavelengths are known precisely from laboratory work. In light from a distant galaxy the **same recognisable pattern** appears, but every line is shifted towards **longer** wavelengths — so the size of the shift can be measured exactly.

**The key observation is a relationship**, and all three parts of it matter: **the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving, and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.**

**What this shows.** An increase in wavelength indicates that the source is **moving away**, so the galaxies are **receding** from us — and the more distant ones are receding faster.

The important interpretation is that **space itself (the universe) is expanding**, rather than galaxies flying outwards through fixed space from some central point. The evidence for that reading is the pattern itself: if galaxies were debris from an explosion at a point, we could locate that point, and we would appear to sit near it. But **every observer in every galaxy** sees the same thing — everything receding, with the most distant fastest.

That is exactly what **uniformly stretching space** predicts. If all distances grow by the same proportion, then from **any** viewpoint the furthest objects recede fastest, simply because there is **more space in between to stretch**. So there is **no centre**, and the further-means-faster relationship is a **prediction** of the model rather than an awkward coincidence — which is why observing it is such strong support.

**How this leads to the Big Bang.** If the universe is expanding now, then in the past everything must have been **closer together**. Running that backwards, the further back one goes the closer everything was, until all the matter converges into a very small volume. Compressing the same matter into a smaller space makes it **denser**, and denser matter is **hotter**.

This leads to the conclusion that **the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense** — the Big Bang theory.

It is worth noting that this is how scientific theories are built: from **observation** to interpretation to model to extrapolation. The theory was not proposed and then defended, but **drawn from the evidence** — and it is accepted because it continues to fit what is measured.

questions.prompt: Explain how observations since 1998 have changed our understanding of the expanding universe, and discuss what remains unknown.
questions.solution:
**Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.**

**How supernovae were used.** A particular type of exploding star has a known and consistent intrinsic brightness. Comparing how bright such a supernova **appears** with how bright it **actually is** gives its **distance**. Combining that distance with its **red-shift** allows astronomers to reconstruct how quickly the universe was expanding at different times in its history, because light from more distant supernovae left them longer ago.

**How this differs from the red-shift evidence.** The two findings are distinct, and it is worth keeping them apart. The original **red-shift** observations established that the universe is **expanding** — that galaxies are receding, and the distant ones fastest. The **supernova** observations, decades later, suggest something further: that the rate of expansion is **increasing**. The universe is not merely expanding but **accelerating**.

**Why this was surprising.** Gravity is an attractive force acting on all matter, so the expectation was that gravity would gradually **slow the expansion down** over time. Finding that it is speeding up instead meant something significant was **missing from the model** — a result that was unexpected enough that it was checked extensively before being accepted.

**What remains unknown.** The specification is explicit that **there is still much about the universe that is not understood**, and gives two examples.

**Dark mass** — often called dark matter — **bends light and holds galaxies together but does not emit electromagnetic radiation**. Because it emits nothing, it cannot be observed directly at any wavelength. Its existence is inferred entirely from its **gravitational effects**: galaxies rotate as though they contain far more mass than is visible, and light passing near them is bent more than the visible matter can account for.

**Dark energy** is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion to accelerate.

**The limitation worth drawing out** is that neither name is an **explanation**. Calling something dark energy records that there is an effect requiring a cause which is not yet identified; it fills a gap in the vocabulary rather than in the understanding. The same is true of dark mass, though at least its gravitational behaviour is well characterised even if its nature is not.

**What this says about science** is the point the specification is really making. The Big Bang model is **very well supported** by multiple independent lines of evidence, and at the same time **large questions about the universe remain open**. Both statements are true simultaneously, and a scientific theory being incomplete is not the same as it being wrong. The supernova results are a good illustration: they did not overturn the expanding universe, but they showed the model was missing something important — and the honest response was to name the gap and keep investigating.

Discusses dark mass and dark energy and what they represent.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.**

**How supernovae were used.** A particular type of exploding star has a known and consistent intrinsic brightness. Comparing how bright such a supernova **appears** with how bright it **actually is** gives its **distance**. Combining that distance with its **red-shift** allows astronomers to reconstruct how quickly the universe was expanding at different times in its history, because light from more distant supernovae left them longer ago.

**How this differs from the red-shift evidence.** The two findings are distinct, and it is worth keeping them apart. The original **red-shift** observations established that the universe is **expanding** — that galaxies are receding, and the distant ones fastest. The **supernova** observations, decades later, suggest something further: that the rate of expansion is **increasing**. The universe is not merely expanding but **accelerating**.

**Why this was surprising.** Gravity is an attractive force acting on all matter, so the expectation was that gravity would gradually **slow the expansion down** over time. Finding that it is speeding up instead meant something significant was **missing from the model** — a result that was unexpected enough that it was checked extensively before being accepted.

**What remains unknown.** The specification is explicit that **there is still much about the universe that is not understood**, and gives two examples.

**Dark mass** — often called dark matter — **bends light and holds galaxies together but does not emit electromagnetic radiation**. Because it emits nothing, it cannot be observed directly at any wavelength. Its existence is inferred entirely from its **gravitational effects**: galaxies rotate as though they contain far more mass than is visible, and light passing near them is bent more than the visible matter can account for.

**Dark energy** is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion to accelerate.

**The limitation worth drawing out** is that neither name is an **explanation**. Calling something dark energy records that there is an effect requiring a cause which is not yet identified; it fills a gap in the vocabulary rather than in the understanding. The same is true of dark mass, though at least its gravitational behaviour is well characterised even if its nature is not.

**What this says about science** is the point the specification is really making. The Big Bang model is **very well supported** by multiple independent lines of evidence, and at the same time **large questions about the universe remain open**. Both statements are true simultaneously, and a scientific theory being incomplete is not the same as it being wrong. The supernova results are a good illustration: they did not overturn the expanding universe, but they showed the model was missing something important — and the honest response was to name the gap and keep investigating.

examTechnique.body:
Define red-shift as an **increase in wavelength**, and give all three parts of the key observation: **further, faster, bigger shift**.

Say **space itself is expanding**, not galaxies flying from a centre, and use the **no-centre** argument. Keep **red-shift (expansion)** apart from **supernovae since 1998 (acceleration)**.
examinerErrors: Defining red-shift as "the light looks red".
Giving distance and speed but omitting the size of the shift.
Saying galaxies fly outwards through space from a centre.
Trying to identify where the centre of the universe is.
Merging the red-shift and supernova evidence into one finding.
Treating dark energy as an explanation rather than a name.
Describing the Big Bang as an explosion within space.
Forgetting that a few nearby galaxies show blue-shift.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer defines red-shift as an **increase in wavelength** and gives the full observation — **further, faster, bigger shift** — because the relationship is what carries the argument. It insists that **space itself is expanding**, and supports that with the **no-centre** reasoning: every observer sees the same pattern, which is what uniform stretching predicts. It explains **further-means-faster** mechanically, by more space stretching, turning a correlation into an explanation. It separates the **red-shift** evidence for expansion from the **supernova** evidence since 1998 for acceleration, notes that the latter was surprising because gravity should have slowed things, and observes that **naming dark energy is not explaining it** — while holding that a well-supported model can still have large gaps in it.
